danishChanges.before: BUDBRINGEREN. Da dine to børn kom med deres far ind i salene, der var pyntet til bryllup, blev vi slaver glade, for vi havde sørget over din ulykke. Straks gik det fra mund til mund, at du og din mand havde sluttet fred. En kyssede børnenes hænder, en anden deres lyse hoveder. Jeg var så glad, at jeg fulgte dem ind i kvindernes værelser. Så rejste hun sig og gik gennem salene med små, lette skridt på sine hvide fødder. Hun glædede sig over gaverne og så igen og igen ned over sig selv fra halsen til kjortlens kant. Så kom det frygtelige syn. Pludselig skiftede hendes ansigt farve. Hun vaklede baglæns, hele kroppen rystede, og hun nåede kun lige at synke ned på en bænk, før hun ellers var faldet på gulvet. En gammel tjenestekvinde troede, at Pan eller en anden gud havde sendt anfaldet, og råbte en bøn. Men så så hun det hvide skum om munden, de rullende øjne og det blodløse ansigt. Nu blev råbet til et langt, højt skrig. En løb til hendes fars værelser, en anden til hendes nye mand for at fortælle om brudens ulykke. Hele huset genlød af løbende fødder. Der gik så lang tid, som en hurtig løber bruger på en bane på seks plethra. Så vågnede den stakkels kvinde fra sin stumme bevidstløshed med et frygteligt skrig. Smerten kom fra to sider som to angribende hære. Guldbåndet om hendes hoved sprøjtede fortærende ild, og den fine kjortel, som dine børn havde bragt, åd hendes hvide kød. Hun sprang op og løb, helt i flammer. Hun rystede hovedet og håret for at få diademet af, men guldet sad fast. Hver gang hun rystede lokkerne, blussede ilden dobbelt så voldsomt. Til sidst faldt hun sammen på gulvet, overvundet af smerte. Kun en far kunne have genkendt hende. Øjnenes stolte ro og ansigtets skønhed var borte. Fra hovedet dryppede blod blandet med ild. Kødet smeltede af knoglerne som harpiks fra et fyrretræ under den gådefulde gifts angreb. Det var frygteligt at se. Ingen turde røre liget. Hendes skæbne havde advaret os. Så kom hendes ulykkelige far ind, endnu uvidende om det hele. Han kastede sig over liget, græd, omfavnede hende og kyssede hende. »Mit stakkels barn,« råbte han, »hvilken gud har ødelagt dig så frygteligt? Hvem har taget dig fra mig, der allerede står med det ene ben i graven? Gid jeg kunne dø sammen med dig!« Da han holdt op med at græde og klage, ville han rejse sig. Men han hang fast i kjortlen som vedbend om laurbærgrene. Så begyndte en rædselsfuld kamp. Når han prøvede at løfte knæet, trak hendes krop ham tilbage. Rev han sig løs med magt, flåede han kødet af sine egne knogler. Til sidst gav han op og døde. Han kunne ikke længere kæmpe imod. Dér ligger ligene, datteren i sin gamle fars arme. Den sorg kan kun tårer udtrykke, ikke ord. Om din del i det vil jeg ikke sige noget. Du må selv finde en vej fra straffen. Men endnu en gang ser jeg, at menneskets liv kun er en skygge. Jeg siger det gerne: De, der regnes for kloge og er dygtige til at tale, er de største tåber. Intet menneske er lykkeligt. Når heldet vender, kan man blive rigere end sin nabo. Men lykkelig? Nej. (Han går.)

englishChanges.before: MESSENGER. When your two children arrived with their father and entered the rooms decorated for the wedding, those of us servants who grieved for your troubles were pleased. News of a truce in the old quarrel between you and your husband immediately began to whisper from ear to ear. One person kissed your sons' hands, another their golden heads. Happiness drew me after them into the women's rooms. The woman we now honoured in your place, before she saw your pair of sons yoked together like a chariot team, kept turning longing eyes towards Jason. Then she drew her veil across her face and twisted her pale neck away contemptuously, disgusted by the approach of your children. Your husband tried to soften the girl's anger and hostility. He said, "Do not treat your friends as enemies. Stop being angry and turn your head back. Regard as friends the people your husband regards as friends. Accept their presents, and ask your father to cancel their exile, for my sake." When she saw the finery, she could not resist and agreed to everything her husband asked. Before the father and your boys had gone far from her room, she took the richly worked clothes and dressed herself, setting the golden crown around her curls. She arranged her hair before a bright mirror, smiling at the phantom image of herself. Then she rose and walked through the rooms, taking dainty steps on ivory feet, delighted with her gifts and repeatedly glancing down from her neck to the hem at her ankles. What followed was terrible to see. Her colour changed suddenly. She staggered backwards, her limbs trembling, and barely managed to drop onto a couch before she fell to the floor. An old serving-woman, thinking perhaps that Pan or another God had sent this seizure, raised a cry of prayer. That was before she noticed the white foam bubbling from the girl's mouth, her rolling eyes and her bloodless face. Then the servant gave a different cry, a long, loud scream. At once one person rushed to her father's rooms, another to her new husband, to tell them the bride had been stricken. The whole house echoed with hurrying feet. By then a fast runner straining every limb could have reached the finish of a six-plethra course. She woke from that speechless trance, her eyes having been shut, and gave a shrill, horrible scream, poor woman! Her agony attacked like two armies charging at once. The golden band round her head began shooting out an astonishing stream of ravenous flame, while the delicate clothes your children had given her devoured her pale flesh. She leapt from the couch and ran, all on fire, shaking her head and hair from side to side to throw off the crown. But the gold clasp gripped her firmly. Whenever she shook her locks, the fire blazed with twice the fury. At last, overcome by suffering, she fell to the floor, so disfigured that only a father could have recognised her. The regal calm of her eyes and her lovely features had disappeared. Blood dripped from the top of her head, mingled with sparks of fire. The flesh melted off her bones like resin dripping from a pine, consumed by that mysterious poison. A dreadful sight! Everyone was afraid to touch the body, warned by her hideous fate. Her miserable father, still knowing nothing of what had happened, suddenly entered and threw himself upon her corpse. He began to wail, wrapped his arms around her body, kissed her and cried, "My unhappy child, what God has destroyed you so horribly? Who has robbed this old man, already a tomb, of you? Ah, if only I could die beside you!" When his tears and groans subsided, he tried to raise his aged body, but he clung to those fine robes as ivy clings around laurel branches. Then came a ghastly struggle. As he tried to lift his knee, her body pulled against him. If he dragged himself away by force, he tore his old flesh from his bones. At last he gave up and breathed his last, the unfortunate man unable to resist his destruction any longer. The bodies lie there, the daughter held in her old father's embrace. Tears must mourn that suffering; words cannot. I shall say nothing about your part in it. You will find your own way to escape punishment. But now, as often before, I consider human life a shadow. I am not afraid to say that those who seem wise among us, those skilled in clever speech, are guilty of the deepest foolishness. No mortal is happy. At the high tide of fortune a man may be more prosperous than his neighbour. But happy? No! (He leaves).

englishChanges.before: JASON. Abomination! Woman most hateful to the Gods, to me and to all humanity, you dared plunge a sword into the little ones you bore and leave me ruined and childless! After doing this, after daring an act so unholy, can you still look upon the earth and sun? May destruction take you! Now I see clearly what I failed to see when I brought you out of a barbarian country and household into a Greek home: a total curse, a traitor to your father and the land that raised you! The Gods have hurled the thunderbolt of your guilt against me. You murdered your own brother beside his hearth before you boarded Argo with its beautiful prow. Those were your beginnings. Then you married me and became my sons' mother, only to murder them for the sake of your marriage rights. No Greek woman would have dared such a deed. Yet I lowered myself to marry you instead of one of them, a hateful, savage bride, a tigress instead of a woman, with a fiercer nature than Scylla of the Tyrrhenian sea. But no amount of abuse could pierce you; your nature is too hardened. Get away, you criminal stained with your children's blood! I can only weep for my destiny. I shall have no happiness with my newly married bride, and never speak alive to the sons I fathered and raised. Lost, lost to me!
